title: How do you implement a gRPC service in Spring Boot — add the `grpc-spring-boot-starter` dependency and the protobuf Maven/Gradle plugin, define your `.proto` file, run code generation, annotate the server implementation with `@GrpcService` (extends the generated `ImplBase`), and inject a client stub with `@GrpcClient("service-name")` — and how does service discovery and health checking integrate (gRPC health checking protocol, Kubernetes gRPC probes, Eureka/Consul)?
shortTitle: How do you implement a gRPC service in Spring Boot, and how do service discovery and health checking integrate?

s1_definition.profdef: Implementing gRPC in Spring Boot uses the `grpc-spring-boot-starter`, which auto-configures a Netty-based gRPC server and client management. You add the protobuf build plugin, define the `.proto`, generate stubs, annotate your server implementation with `@GrpcService` so it registers automatically, and inject a client stub into another bean with `@GrpcClient("service-name")`. Service discovery integrates by resolving that logical service name through a registry such as Eureka or Consul, or through Kubernetes DNS, so the client finds live instances. Health checking uses the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol, a built-in `grpc.health.v1.Health` service, which Kubernetes can probe with a native gRPC liveness and readiness probe.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India wiring up a new department. The grpc-spring-boot-starter is the office manager who automatically sets up the phone line and the reception desk the moment you hire a department, so you just annotate the department as open for business with @GrpcService. When another department needs to call it, it simply asks for it by name with @GrpcClient, and the building directory (Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes DNS) tells it which rooms currently have staff. The health check is the daily roll call: a supervisor periodically asks each department "are you ready to serve?" and routes customers only to the ones that say yes.
s1_definition.oneliner: @GrpcService registers the server and @GrpcClient injects the stub, a registry or Kubernetes DNS resolves the service name, and the standard gRPC health protocol lets Kubernetes probe readiness natively.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Implementing gRPC in Spring Boot uses the `grpc-spring-boot-starter`, which auto-configures a Netty-based gRPC server and client management. You add the protobuf build plugin, define the `.proto`, generate stubs, annotate your server implementation with `@GrpcService` so it registers automatically, and inject a client stub into another bean with `@GrpcClient("service-name")`. Service discovery integrates by resolving that logical service name through a registry such as Eureka or Consul, or through Kubernetes DNS, so the client finds live instances. Health checking uses the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol, a built-in `grpc.health.v1.Health` service, which Kubernetes can probe with a native gRPC liveness and readiness probe.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India wiring up a new department. The grpc-spring-boot-starter is the office manager who automatically sets up the phone line and the reception desk the moment you hire a department, so you just annotate the department as open for business with @GrpcService. When another department needs to call it, it simply asks for it by name with @GrpcClient, and the building directory (Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes DNS) tells it which rooms currently have staff. The health check is the daily roll call: a supervisor periodically asks each department "are you ready to serve?" and routes customers only to the ones that say yes.

**One line to remember:** @GrpcService registers the server and @GrpcClient injects the stub, a registry or Kubernetes DNS resolves the service name, and the standard gRPC health protocol lets Kubernetes probe readiness natively.

sections.s2_technical:
You add the `grpc-spring-boot-starter` dependency, often the one from the net.devh project, plus the protobuf Maven or Gradle plugin and the gRPC Java plugin so the build generates stubs from your `.proto`. The starter autoconfigures an embedded gRPC server on a configured port, separate from the HTTP port, and scans for beans annotated with `@GrpcService`. Your server class extends the generated `ImplBase` and carries `@GrpcService`, so it is registered with the server with zero boilerplate. For example `@GrpcService public class TransferGrpcService extends TransferServiceGrpc.TransferServiceImplBase { ... }`.

On the client side you inject a stub into any Spring bean with `@GrpcClient("account-service")`, where the name matches a client entry in `application.yml` under `grpc.client`. For example `@GrpcClient("account-service") private TransferServiceGrpc.TransferServiceBlockingStub stub;`. The configuration tells it the address and negotiation type, and you call the stub like a normal method. The starter also supports global and per-client interceptors for cross-cutting concerns.

For discovery, instead of a static address you point the client at a discovery-backed address. With Eureka or Consul the starter can resolve `discovery:///account-service` to live registered instances; with Kubernetes you use the headless service DNS so the client sees all pod IPs and can client-side load balance across them. Health checking uses the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol, which defines a `Health` service with a `Check` method returning SERVING or NOT_SERVING and a `Watch` for streaming updates. The starter can expose this service automatically, and Kubernetes 1.24 and later supports a native gRPC probe, so you configure `grpc: { port: 9090 }` in the readiness and liveness probe and Kubernetes calls the Health service directly instead of needing a custom exec script. A senior nuance: tie the health status to real readiness, for example report NOT_SERVING while the database connection pool is still warming up, so traffic is not routed to a pod that will fail; and prefer client-side load balancing with the Kubernetes headless service for gRPC, because a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection through an L4 load balancer would otherwise pin all calls to one pod.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to add a gRPC transfer service without hand-writing server bootstrapping and connection management, and have other services call it by name. This is exactly what the grpc-spring-boot-starter solves — annotate with @GrpcService to expose it and @GrpcClient to consume it.

Problem 2 — The service runs as several pods that scale up and down, and the bank must route calls only to healthy, ready instances and spread load evenly. This is exactly what service discovery plus the gRPC health protocol solve — discovery finds live pods and the health check tells Kubernetes which are ready.

The demo shows the transfer proto, a @GrpcService implementation, a @GrpcClient caller, the application.yml wiring discovery and health, and a health service tied to real readiness. Classes and steps: `transfer.proto`, `TransferGrpcService`, `TransferGrpcClient`, `ReadinessHealthIndicator`, and the YAML.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build (protobuf plugin generates stubs, starter wires the server)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run (embedded gRPC server starts on 9090 automatically)
java -jar target/grpc-springboot-transfer-1.0.0.jar

# Verify health via the standard gRPC Health protocol
grpc_health_probe -addr=localhost:9090        # returns SERVING

# Inspect services with reflection
grpcurl -plaintext localhost:9090 list

# In Kubernetes, the native gRPC readiness probe calls grpc.health.v1.Health/Check
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the transfer service starts as a pod, and another service calls it by name to transfer Rs.50,000 from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1 — On startup the grpc-spring-boot-starter scans for @GrpcService beans, finds TransferGrpcService, and registers it on the embedded gRPC server on port 9090, and it exposes the standard Health service.

Step 2 — The ReadinessHealthIndicator first sets the health status to NOT_SERVING, warms up the database pool, then sets it to SERVING. Kubernetes calls the native gRPC readiness probe, sees SERVING, and begins routing traffic to this pod.

Step 3 — The calling service's @GrpcClient resolves account-service through the Kubernetes headless DNS, discovers the live pod IPs, and uses round-robin client-side load balancing to pick one, then calls stub.transfer with the request.

Step 4 — TransferGrpcService receives the typed request, debits Rajesh to Rs.950,000, credits Priya to Rs.300,000, and returns COMPLETED. If the pod had reported NOT_SERVING, Kubernetes would not have sent the call to it in the first place.

```
2026-10-26 15:30:01 [INFO] gRPC health set to SERVING
2026-10-26 15:30:03 [INFO] Transfer Rs.50000 SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 15:30:03 [INFO] Transfer TXF-7b1e... status=COMPLETED
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Startup:
    grpc-spring-boot-starter scans beans → finds @GrpcService TransferGrpcService
      → registers on embedded server :9090  + exposes grpc.health.v1.Health
    ReadinessHealthIndicator: NOT_SERVING → warm DB pool → SERVING
      ▲ K8s readiness probe (grpc:9090) sees SERVING → add pod to endpoints

  Call:
    Caller @GrpcClient("account-service")
      │ resolve dns:///account-service...svc → pod IPs [10.0.1.4, 10.0.1.5]
      │ round_robin pick → 10.0.1.4:9090
      ▼ gRPC / HTTP/2
    TransferGrpcService.transfer(req, obs)
      │ SAV2001 1,000,000→950,000 ; CUR3001 250,000→300,000
      ▼
    TransferResponse(COMPLETED)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Spring Boot gRPC Wiring ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Dependency Injection: @GrpcService bean, @GrpcClient stub      │
  │    WHY: no manual server bootstrap or channel management       │
  │ Service Locator/Discovery: resolve name → live instances       │
  │    WHY: pods scale; address must not be hard-coded             │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: service transfers; health indicator reports readiness       │
  │ O: add a new @GrpcService = new bean, no wiring edits          │
  │ D: caller depends on injected stub abstraction, not transport  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Discovery + Health (as prose) ─────────────────────────────
  discovery  : dns:///svc (K8s) or discovery:///svc (Eureka/Consul)
  LB         : client-side round_robin over resolved pod IPs
  health     : grpc.health.v1.Health Check → SERVING/NOT_SERVING
  K8s probe  : native grpc:{port} readiness + liveness (1.24+)
  readiness  : NOT_SERVING until DB pool warm → then SERVING

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. startup: scan @GrpcService → register on :9090 + Health
  2.   → health NOT_SERVING → warm DB → SERVING → K8s routes
  3.   → caller @GrpcClient resolves name → pod IPs → round_robin
  4.   → stub.transfer → TransferGrpcService.transfer → COMPLETED
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To implement a gRPC service in Spring Boot I add the grpc-spring-boot-starter and the protobuf build plugin with the gRPC Java plugin, define my proto file, and let the build generate the stubs and server base classes. The starter autoconfigures an embedded gRPC server on its own port and scans for beans annotated with @GrpcService. So my server class simply extends the generated ImplBase and carries @GrpcService, and it is registered automatically with no bootstrapping code. To consume it from another service I inject a stub into any bean with @GrpcClient naming the service, and a matching entry in application.yml gives the address and negotiation type, so I just call the stub like a local method.

Service discovery is where the client stops using a hard-coded address and instead resolves the logical service name to live instances. With Eureka or Consul the client resolves something like discovery slash slash slash account-service to the registered instances, and in Kubernetes I point it at the headless service DNS so it sees all the pod IPs and can client-side load balance across them with a round-robin policy. That client-side load balancing matters specifically for gRPC, because a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection through a plain layer-four load balancer would pin every call to one pod.

Health checking uses the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol, which is a built-in Health service with a Check method that returns SERVING or NOT_SERVING and a Watch for streaming updates. The starter can expose this automatically, and from Kubernetes 1.24 onward there is a native gRPC probe, so my readiness and liveness probes just say grpc on the port and Kubernetes calls the Health service directly instead of needing a custom script.

In my banking work at National Bank of India the transfer service ran as several pods, and this wiring meant other services called it simply by name, Kubernetes routed traffic only to ready pods, and load spread evenly across them. The senior detail I always add is to tie the reported health to real readiness: I keep the status NOT_SERVING until the database connection pool is warmed up and only then flip it to SERVING, so Kubernetes never routes a transfer to a pod that would immediately fail, and I pair that with client-side round-robin load balancing over the headless service so one HTTP/2 connection does not pin all traffic to a single instance.
